Everything you need to profitably scale an ecom brand with Google Ads and YouTube Ads in one tweet:

(Bookmark this.)

📂 Google Ads:

📁 Search Campaigns

- Branded search (exact match)
- Non-branded search (phrase match)
- Competitor search (exact match on brand name)
- Problem-aware search (TOF queries sent to advertorial pages)
- Dynamic search ads (let Google find queries you missed)

📁 Shopping Campaigns

- Branded shopping (exclude non-brand)
- Prospecting shopping (best sellers at low tROAS)
- Testing shopping (new products, separate budget)
- Angle-specific shopping (duplicated listings)

📁 PMax

- Remarketing PMax (HIGH tROAS)
- Feed-only PMax (let product feed cook)
- Full-asset PMax (text, image, video, everything)
- Brand exclusion setup (negative keywords in exact match)
- tROAS split (high on PMax, low on prospecting shopping)

📁 Demand Gen

- Lookalike audiences (customer match upload)
- Custom intent audiences (feed Google the search terms)
- In-market audiences (Google's categorisation of active shoppers)
- Remarketing audiences (video viewers, site visitors, cart abandoners across YouTube)
- Asset group separation (never blend audience types in one asset group)

📂 YouTube Ads

- 6-second bumpers (unskippable)
- 15-second in-stream skippable (MOF warm)
- 30-second in-stream (BOF remarketing, UGC style)
- Shorts ads (vertical 9:16, runs in the Shorts feed, colder ICP)
- Custom intent targeting (people who recently searched your category)
- Placement targeting (ads on specific YouTube videos or channels)

📁 Google Merchant Center

- Title optimisation (brand, product, attributes)
- Description optimisation (5,000 chars of search-relevant keywords)
- Image split testing (lifestyle vs studio, duplicate listings to test, lifestyle wins)
- Sale pricing (struck-through original + green sale price, free conversion rate lift)
- Review feed integration (star ratings on Shopping cards, 2-4 week processing time)
- Feed completeness (GTIN, product type, colour, size, material, custom labels for grouping)
- Regional targeting (separate feeds per country if you sell internationally)
- Shipping accuracy (wrong shipping times = GMC suspension)

📁 Bidding Progression

- 0 conversions: maximise clicks with CPC cap
- ~15 conversions: maximise conversion value
- ~30/month consistent: tROAS (LOW on prospecting)
- Branded campaigns: manual CPC or target impression share, ALWAYS
- Budget scaling: 15-20% every 2-3 days, multi-window analysis (7, 14, 30-day), one KPI

📁 Landing Pages

- Transactional traffic: PDP or collection page, short, product-focused
- Informational traffic: advertorial or editorial, long, education-first
- Comparison traffic: "us vs them" page, credibility-first, objective tone
- Quiz funnel: embedded quiz before PDP, personalised recommendation, 1.5-2.5x conversion rate lift
- Above the fold: headline matching search query, benefit subheadline, result image rather than product image, one CTA button

📁 Ad Copy Framework

- Branded: reasons to buy now, offers, clarity
- Transactional: match the search query, social proof
- Comparison: lead with credibility rather than sales copy
- Informational: lead with education, speak to the research process
- H1 mirrors the search, H2 carries the benefit, H3 carries proof or offer

📁 AI Creative Formats

- Claymation (2-3x CTR, warm tactile aesthetic, beats slop fatigue)
- Pixar-style 3D (premium positioning, high recall, mass-market)
- Balloon world (maximum novelty, crowded market pattern break)
- Musical/singing (highest share rate, TikTok-viral jingles)
- Famous cartoon style (nostalgia activation, family/children products)
- UGC-style AI (social proof, remarketing, hybrid production)
- Cinematic product film (high-ticket justification, brand halo)

📁 AI Tool Stack

- Opus 5 for scripts, prompts, analysis, decisions ($5/$25 per Mtok)
- GPT Images 2.0 for 2K frames (99% text accuracy, agentic reasoning)
- Seedance 2.0 via Higgsfield MCP for animation (native audio, cinematic physics)
- Google Ads MCP (Markifact or Adspirer) for campaign management from Claude

📁 Account Health Signals

- Search Top IS (your rank position vs competitors)
- Search Lost IS by rank (you're being aggressively outbid)
- Search Lost IS by budget (your budget is exhausted before demand is)
- New customer ROAS (the actual prospecting number rather than the blended figure)
- Attribution clarity (branded and non-branded completely separated, always)
- MER (total revenue / total spend, the full-funnel health check)

📁 Funnel Deployment Order

- Phase 1: branded search + branded shopping + non-branded shopping (BOF)
- Phase 2: prospecting shopping + non-branded search + PMax remarketing (MOF)
- Phase 3: Demand Gen + YouTube Ads + TOF search (TOF)
- Always bottom up. Never launch TOF before MOF works.

This is the full map. Every campaign type and format.

The brands printing $100k+ days on Google are pulling from this exact system.

The brands sitting flat at $10k/month are missing 80% of the map.

NEW RESEARCH: You can now create a new robot optimized for any given task!

I love this new project by @haqhuy, @SongShuran, and others.

Called "Transformer Transformer: A Unified Model for Motion-Conditioned Robot Co-design", it generates a robot's physical design and its controller together from a task spec.

DEFINITIONS:
- Reward function: A scoring rule that assigns a number to how well a behavior achieves the task. Here, it is the objective the generated design is pushed to maximize (e.g., track the target motion with low error).
- Tokenizing: dividing continuous or structured data (a robot's links, joints, motor specs, states, actions) into a discrete vocabulary of symbols a transformer can process, the same step that turned pixels and audio into "language" for these models.
- Diffusion transformer (DiT): A transformer trained to turn random noise into structured output through iterative denoising. Here, it generates robot bodies and trajectories instead of images.
- MuJoCo: The standard fast physics simulator for robotics research (DeepMind-maintained). The Menagerie is its curated zoo of ready-to-use robot models.
- CMA-ES: Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy, the workhorse black-box optimizer: it evolves a population of candidate designs, keeps the best, and needs thousands of simulator rollouts.
- Bimanual multi-trajectory optimization: Finding one design/controller that performs well across several target motions for a two-armed robot at once, harder than optimizing for a single arm and a single motion.
- BERT/MAE masked-modeling trick: Train one model to fill in whatever parts of the input you hide (words for BERT, image patches for MAE); at inference, choosing what to mask chooses the task, so masking the body makes it a designer and masking the actions makes it a controller.

In practice, you give it a target end-effector motion and a reward function, and it outputs a complete embodiment (link, joint, motor, and inertial property), as well as a controller to drive it.

It works by tokenizing both the body (links/joints/motors) and the dynamics (states/actions) into a compact scheme called RoboTokens, training a diffusion transformer (DiT) over them.
The same model predicts dynamics using those predictions ("Dynamics Self-Guidance") to push generated designs toward higher reward at inference time.
Masking different token types (using the BERT/MAE masked-modeling trick) lets the one model do three jobs: generate an embodiment, control an arbitrary embodiment, or design one conditioned on a motion.

It is trained on 11 robots from the MuJoCo Menagerie (0.65 kg hand to 67.5 kg quadruped, 6–35 joints), and validated in sim and on a physical ALOHA doing cloth flinging.

I like the fact that this approach inverts the entire recent robotics ideas: designing a policy for a fixed robot -> designing the robot for a fixed task.
Every other approach assumes the body is given and learns a controller.
Transformer Transformer takes the task (target motion + reward), then generates the body and controller jointly.

In practice, it is a ~180× speedup over the standard optimizer at equal-or-better quality.
It reaches "CMA-ES-level quality in seconds" and finishes bimanual multi-trajectory optimization in <1 min vs CMA-ES's 3+ hours.

Surprisingly, this approach was validated on real hardware!
The generated design was measurably smoother.
On a physical ALOHA flinging cloth (a deformable, dynamic task), the optimized design cut tracking error 73% and peak joint speed 30% versus the original, with fewer joint-speed peaks.
Therefore: real world results, not a sim-only benchmark -> that is worth underlining nowadays!

Also worth mentioning: this is the lab behind UMI and Handroid, that I mentioned here previously!
The team seems extremely creative, i love these out-of-the-box approaches.

Some people are surprised that APIs (aka what Anthropic, OpenAI, and others provide) are treated differently than open weights in the new AI model framework. 

I'm not surprised at all, and it's actually very good policy. Let me explain:

Model weights, APIs, and apps are three very different layers of the stack. Treating them the same would be a recipe for bad regulation.

Think about how we handle cars. We don't regulate steel, we crash-test cars. Nobody asks a steel mill to guarantee that nothing dangerous will ever be built with its steel. Obligations sit with the carmaker and rules of the road with the driver, because that's where risk becomes real and where someone can actually act on it.

Model weights are the steel of AI. They're raw research output, closer to science than product: no user, no interface, no deployment. They don't do anything on their own. And because everything else is built on top of them, this is the layer where regulation does the most damage. Restrict weights and you slow down all progress downstream, and you prevent countless positive use cases from ever emerging: the lab fine-tuning an open model for rare diseases, the startup serving a language big providers ignore, the safety researchers who can only audit models because the weights are open. You don't reduce risk, you just kill open source and concentrate power in a few big labs.

APIs are the middle layer, the parts and engine suppliers of AI: a commercial service where a provider serves a model at scale. Here you have a business relationship, terms of service, the ability to monitor for abuse. It makes sense to expect transparency, security standards, and accountability from providers at this layer, because they can actually enforce things.

Apps are the car on the road: where AI meets the real world. A medical assistant, a hiring tool, a companion for kids, a financial advisor. This is where concrete harm can happen, and conveniently, it's where we already have decades of regulation. Health, finance, employment, consumer protection. An AI hiring tool should comply with employment law whether it's powered by an open model, an API, or a spreadsheet.

The principle is simple: regulate at the layer where risk actually materializes and where actors can act on it. Push obligations to the deployment layer, keep the research layer open. We don't regulate steel, we crash-test cars. Well done @realDonaldTrump @DavidSacks @mkratsios47!

Something about this CNPYNetwork demo genuinely changed how I think about building onchain.

One of their engineers opened Claude, described a prediction market, and roughly twenty minutes later there was a working version running as its own virtual chain.

Not a smart contract sitting on someone else’s blockspace.

An actual chain with its own state and rules.

And honestly, the 20 minutes is not even the part I find most interesting.

It is what made those 20 minutes possible.

Canopy’s template reduces the core chain stack to roughly 200 lines of readable code, covering things like consensus, security, and deployment.

That is small enough for an AI tool to actually understand what it is working with.

So instead of spending hours fighting infrastructure before you even get to the product, you can describe what you want to build and start working on the application itself.

You still need to understand what you are building, of course.

But the barrier between having an idea and actually running it is getting much smaller.

There is also something important about ownership here.

The chain gets security through Canopy’s recursive restaking model, can remain nested, or eventually stand on its own.

That means you are not simply building an application on somebody else’s chain and accepting whatever limitations come with it.

You can build your own environment around the product.

That is why the line “AI creates apps, Canopy creates owners” makes a lot more sense after seeing the demo.

The interesting part is not that AI can write code.

We already know that.

The interesting part is what happens when AI can help you create the entire environment your application runs in.

Watch the 20 minute demo.

Then try building something yourself.

That is probably where this gets really interesting.

My honest opinion here: everyone’s watched someone vibe-code a UI mockup by now, that part isn’t news anymore. What’s actually different is watching that same speed apply to something that ends up as a fully deployed, sovereign onchain product, not a prototype that dies in a sandbox

What stands out to me about this specific example:
→ A prediction market isn’t a toy app, it’s logic-heavy, needs real infrastructure, and still got built in 20 minutes
→ It didn’t stop at “code generated,” it went all the way to deployed as its own virtual chain, no separate infra step required
→ This is one of @CNPYNetwork ’s own devs proving the Templates thesis on the exact use case skeptics usually point to as “too complex for AI to handle”

I think the honest reason people haven’t tried this yet isn’t doubt about the tech, it’s just not having tried it themselves. Watching is a completely different experience from doing

20 minutes is a low enough bar that “I’ll try it eventually” stops being a real excuse

If you built anything in the next 20 minutes with AI, what would it be?

A 21-YEAR-OLD CHINESE GIRL MAKES $12,000+ A MONTH WITH A DANCING ANIME GIRL THAT DOESN’T EVEN EXIST

No, I’m not talking about game development or animation.

She simply dances in front of a camera.

AI turns every movement, facial expression, and gesture into a realistic anime avatar that copies her perfectly.

That’s the version she posts online. Not herself.

Millions of people follow the character. Most of them don’t even care who’s controlling it.

Fashion brands pay the avatar to wear their clothes. Beauty companies pay the avatar to promote their products. Gaming studios pay the avatar to appear in campaigns.

The audience never bought into the AI. They bought into the personality.

That’s the biggest misconception about AI creators.

People don’t follow technology. They follow characters they enjoy watching.

The creators who understand that first will build the next generation of internet celebrities.

The future of product marketing is not about taking better photos. It's about creating campaigns that people can't stop watching.
